assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection changed how trade is modelled. It showed that gains from trade operate through reallocation across firms, not only across industries, and it supports a large empirical and quantitative literature. The conceptual change is deep and reaches well beyond trade.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution. Helpman, with Melitz and Yeaple, and earlier with Krugman on monopolistic competition and trade, gives the intellectual lineage and the proximity/concentration and FDI extensions. Redding's quantitative spatial and trade work is substantial but later and more derivative, so I leave him out of the core credit.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of replication, extension and use in policy and measurement. This is ample time for confirmation.
uncertainties: Krugman's 2008 prize already covers part of the new-trade-theory territory.
Whether the committee prefers to include Redding or Yeaple, who is not on the list.
Helpman's separate work on trade and politics (B046) overlaps with this candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: These authors founded modern political economics. They built formal models of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy, and tested them empirically with comparative data. Their work links economic theory to the study of institutions and is widely used.
assessment.attribution: The credit is shared among three authors who wrote both individually and jointly. Persson-Tabellini (Political Economics, 2000; constitutions and policy) and Besley-Persson (state capacity, 'Pillars of Prosperity') are tightly linked bodies of work. Three names is the natural number.
assessment.maturity: Developed over thirty years, with a stable and well-tested empirical record.
uncertainties: The 2024 prize on institutions and prosperity (Acemoglu, Johnson, Robinson) is adjacent, so the committee may see thematic overlap.
Some causal claims about electoral rules rest on cross-country identification that is open to challenge.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the 'China shock' evidence changed how economists think about labour demand, polarisation and the local costs of trade. The work is empirically careful, uses new data and has had large effects on policy debate.
assessment.attribution: Autor-Dorn-Hanson (2013) is the core of the China shock literature. Autor's earlier task-based work with Levy and Murnane, and with Katz, is foundational but spans several authors. The theory of tasks (Acemoglu-Autor) overlaps with prior prizes. Three names fit the empirical trade-shock core.
assessment.maturity: More than a decade of testing. The magnitude and persistence of the effects are still debated.
uncertainties: Replication and interpretation of the China shock magnitudes, including exposure measures and the role of automation.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on technological change and growth, and with the earlier institutional prize, in how the committee frames the field.
Credit for the task framework is split with Acemoglu, who has already won.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The top-income series built from tax records opened a new long-run view of inequality and reoriented public debate and empirical work in many countries. It is a measurement contribution of the first rank, and I value it particularly as historical-data construction combined with economic reasoning.
assessment.attribution: Piketty-Saez (2003) is the foundational contribution. Zucman's work on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts is important but later. Atkinson, a key early pioneer, is deceased and cannot be credited. Saez also appears under B003 and B011-adjacent topics, which spreads his credit across candidates.
assessment.maturity: Two decades of use, with the World Inequality Database now institutionalised. The theoretical claims in Capital in the Twenty-First Century are less settled than the measurement.
uncertainties: Methodological critiques of capital-income and wealth-share estimates.
Whether the committee treats the measurement contribution as sufficient without a stronger theory result.
Zucman's exclusion from the proposed laureates is a close call because his contributions are important but more recent.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The misallocation framework gave a tractable, measurable account of why some countries are poorer, tied to micro data on firm-level distortions. It changed development accounting and the study of productivity differences.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) is the central paper. Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) is a parallel founding paper, but Rogerson is not on the credited list. Restuccia is credited here. The attribution is therefore somewhat unstable, and I propose the pair with the strongest single-paper claim.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of use. The framework is widely applied, though measurement of distortions is contested.
uncertainties: Sensitivity of measured misallocation to measurement error and to model assumptions.
The absence of Rogerson from the credited names weakens a clean attribution.
Distortions are inferred as residuals, not identified causally.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The World Management Survey and the field experiment in Indian textile firms showed that management practices explain a measurable share of productivity differences. This links micro evidence on firms to productivity and growth.
assessment.attribution: Bloom and Van Reenen led the measurement and the experiments. Sadun is a significant collaborator, but I treat her role as secondary. Bloom also appears in B007 (uncertainty), so credit is spread across two candidates.
assessment.maturity: About twenty years of work, with growing replication across countries. Causal evidence from experiments is limited to a few settings.
uncertainties: External validity of the Indian experiment and of survey-based management scores.
Whether the committee sees the contribution as a research programme more than a single decisive discovery.
Bloom's work is divided between two candidate prizes.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-wide administrative data made it possible to measure intergenerational mobility by place and to study neighbourhood effects, with strong policy relevance. The data approach is a methodological advance in empirical public economics.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is central to the whole programme. Hendren is the leading co-author on the place-effects and childhood-exposure work. Friedman and Katz are important co-authors, but the credit is dispersed. Chetty appears in several candidates (B003, B011), which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: The main results date from about 2014 onward. The programme is influential but still young, and some findings have not been fully replicated or have been challenged.
uncertainties: Causal interpretation of place effects and sensitivity to methodological critiques.
The work may be too recent for a Nobel Prize of a mature, confirmed discovery.
Credit is spread across a large team and across several candidates.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework underpin modern monetary-policy analysis and central-bank practice. The importance is very high, but many different contributors share the credit.
assessment.attribution: Taylor (staggered contracts, the Taylor rule) and Calvo (time-dependent pricing) built the foundations. Woodford synthesised the framework. Gali, Gertler, Christiano and Eichenbaum made major contributions, such as estimated DSGE models, that cannot all fit within three names. Any selection of three is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Highly mature, with decades of use and the lessons of the financial crisis and the 2021-23 inflation. Some of the framework's limits have been exposed.
uncertainties: Diffuse attribution among eight credited names.
Prior prizes for macro and monetary policy (Bernanke, Kydland-Prescott, Phelps) cover parts of the field.
Performance of the framework during the post-pandemic inflation, and challenges from heterogeneous-agent models.
